questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academic reputation, especially in the field of International Relations and the city of London.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, KCL has a weekly newsletter for more than four months pre-arrival and they provide mandatory webinars. I thought it got a bit repetitive even.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None outside the ordinary international check-in and some advice regarding what courses I could take.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
They were difficult about my english proficiency certificate which I had to redo, otherwise no issues.

I would have liked more in-person welcoming events

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Student housing is limited for a six month period but students at London universities also go on exchange and they will post their rooms in university related FB-groups (I found my room through a KCL group even though it was LSE-housing. They are open to all London students.)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Even though it can be very hard to find and quite expensive, I would have liked to stay even further out of city 'Centre' (I stayed in Waterloo). London is by far the nicest in the neighbourhoods along the centre's perimeters.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was really really expensive and very 'studenty' but then again, it was comfortable, warm(!!) and very very central.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The systen is extremely old fashioned and therefore a bit confusing and slow.

You choose from courses in the INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE COURSE CATALOGUE (I didn't know this when I signed up and it limited the available courses by a large amount...) and have to upload them all WITH TIME AND DATE in a form which opens at a specific time and date in november/december (for sem 2). It is very important to be super quick and to have checked all classes for clashes etc. because they will assign you without checking clashes and your availability. It is all your responsibility.

They then manually go through everyones wishes (this takes extremely long, so you will get your courses JUST BEFORE the semester begins)

You then have two weeks to change courses if things don't work out. This worked quite well for me though I missed the two first weeks of two courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: An email inbox with 1-2 days of response time.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: There were many timetable clashes so it just wasn't possible but I ended up with quite nice courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Reach out to someone who has visited KCL about the course registration. I think everyone would miss some kind of rule. Information is not the easiest to find.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level is overall quite comparable to UCPH, though it differs between teachers and classes. I think the seminars can be challenging if you get a good professor and some ambitious fellows but it is also allowed to sit back and listen. I liked taking part in the discussions for the most part.

Grading can be harsh and demanding (though failing is really not very common). They expect more reading outside the syllabus than at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Classes were a similar size.

Discussions were less theoretical and more opinionated.

Essays were more theoretical and less assignment/article-like than at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Even though the teaching really wasn't good (we unfortunately had a substitute teacher) people are really nice in the comparative literature classes. It was a perfect opportunity for me to try a course in a different field (you are allowed 50% of your courses outside the agreed department).

FOREIGN POLICIES OF THE EUROPEAN UNION was the most theoretically engaging if you are looking for the classical English interrogating style of teaching. I really enjoyed it.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Housing was very very expensive but the private market is a hassle (I went through three interviews and was overbid on rent on two...). 
Many sights are very very expensive (standard ticket prises can be >20£ most places) but you can always stick with the parks and free museums of London.
Travelling by train around the country is quite expensive but get a Railcard! It works much better than everyone says!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was less expensive than I thought (slightly cheaper than CPH)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds but memberships are often paid and many unions seemed quite dead/closed off

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Nordic Society is a nice way of meeting people. Some societies hold regular events but I never got fully into one. Beers after class in a pub was always good!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Many many things. You could stay in London and not see nearly everything. I went to Scotland many times (trains are very nice and quick!). Bath and Brighton are nice too. The Cotswolds and Cornwall are worth it in the summer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Beer in the pub!

Otherwise, please ask them to go. Many local students are very quickly out of class and headed somewhere so it can be difficult to get to know them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: London as a city is very hectic compared to almost everything.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are extremely kind, talkative and helpful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Look up classes early on IN THE EXHANGE CATALOGUE (and before applying)

Participate in seminar discussions. Otherwise it will be very boring in the UK

Begin assignments early as they require loads of outside reading.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Find someone who has visited. I think it is only social sciences so check in the FB groups.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The essaywriting is phenomenal. Much better experience than at home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding housing and meeting people in such a busy place as London.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
